body.heading: Chores are the practice hiding in plain sight
paragraphs: Mindfulness is often pictured on a cushion in a quiet room, which makes it sound like another appointment to keep. But the skill itself — being where you are, attending to what is actually happening — can be practised anywhere, and chores are ideal: repetitive, sensory, and already in your day.

Washing-up is the classic example. It has warm water, textures, sounds, small completions, and a clear end. Done on autopilot it is a chore. Done with attention it is ten quiet minutes that happen to produce clean plates.

body.heading: How to wash up mindfully
paragraphs: Feel the water’s temperature and the weight of each item. Hear the sounds — the clink, the splash, the squeak of clean glass. Watch the bubbles do their brief, iridescent work. When you notice you have drifted into planning or replaying, that noticing is the practice; return to the next plate.
Go a little slower than efficiency demands. This is not about washing up badly on purpose; it is about letting one ordinary task be done at human speed, with a human actually present for it.

body.heading: Any chore can take the role
paragraphs: Folding laundry, sweeping, weeding, wiping a table — anything repetitive and safe can host the same practice. Choose one chore to be “yours” for this and let the others stay ordinary. One attended chore a day is a real mindfulness habit, disguised as housework.
There is a side benefit people rarely mention: attended chores stop feeling stolen. The ten minutes were going to be spent anyway. Now they are spent somewhere you actually were.

takeaway: Pick one daily chore and do it with all of your attention; the plates are a bonus.
